title: Practical Plasma Physics: Lasers, Transport, and Magnetisation
text:
1 Introduction
Plasma physics sits at the crossroads of kinetic theory, electromagnetism, fluid dynamics, and statistical mechanics. Nearly 99 % of the visible universe is in the plasma state, and laboratory plasmas underpin technologies ranging from fluorescent lighting to next‑generation accelerators and fusion‑energy concepts. This online book is an introduction to plasma physics from the point of view of transport, lasers and non-local theory. While there are many good introductory textbooks on plasma physics theory, herein the focus is on the practical aspects of plasma physics, with an emphasis on transport phenomena and the use of lasers in plasma experiments: the regimes of high-energy-density physics (HED). Such conditions are routinely accessed at facilities like the National Ignition Facility (NIF), OMEGA, and the Laser Mégajoule (LMJ), where nanosecond laser pulses generate plasmas exceeding tens of mega‑kelvin and magnetic fields of several tens of Tesla. It is therefore not a comprehensive textbook on plasma physics, but rather a resource for those interested in the applications of plasma physics in the context of laser-plasma interactions and transport phenomena.
The book is structured to provide a comprehensive overview of the key concepts and applications in plasma physics. The material is intended for senior undergraduates, graduate students, and early‑career researchers in physics or engineering who have a working knowledge of electrodynamics, statistical mechanics, and vector calculus. The content is designed to be accessible to students and researchers who may not have a deep background in plasma physics but are interested in its applications in the regime of collisional and magnetised plasmas, particularly in the context of HED physics.
In Chapter 2 we introduce the basic concepts of plasma kinetic theory and the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation, from which we derive the equations of magneto-hydrodynamics (MHD): the theory of electrically conducting fluids in the presence of magnetic fields. This is a fundamental aspect of plasma physics, as it describes how plasmas interact with magnetic fields and how these interactions can lead to various phenomena such as magnetic confinement and plasma instabilities. In Chapter 3 we derive the collision operator for plasmas, and how this operator can be used to describe the transport of particles, momentum and energy in plasmas. Collisional processes in plasmas also allow us to introduce the closure of the fluid equations and derive the expressions for thermal transport and Ohm’s law. Chapter 4 builds on the previous chapter to introduce the transport coefficients and how they can be used to describe the anisotropic transport of particles, momentum and energy in plasmas in the presence of magnetic fields. This chapter further discusses important transport processes and phenomena that occur in the collisional and magnetised regime. When the electron distribution in a plasma is significantly far from a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, the local transport approximation breaks down and one must incorporate new models to explain non-local transport. When collisional mean‑free paths approach macroscopic scale‑lengths, classical transport fails. Chapter 5 introduces non-local transport theory and several models that implement corrections to standard local MHD. This chapter also discusses the limitations of the local transport approximation and how non-local transport theory can provide a more accurate description of plasma behaviour in certain regimes.
The focus of this book is also the application of plasma physics in the context of laser-plasma interactions. In Chapter 6 we introduce some of the basic principles of laser propagation relevant to their interactions with plasmas. Chapter 7 will then discuss the interaction of lasers with plasmas, including the mechanisms of energy transfer and the effects of laser-plasma interactions on plasma behaviour. This chapter will also cover some of the important instabilities and phenomena that can arise in laser-plasma interactions, such as stimulated Raman scattering. In Chapter 8, we will explore some of the practical applications of plasma physics in the context of laser-plasma interactions, including inertial confinement fusion. This chapter will highlight the importance of plasma physics in advancing our understanding of fundamental physical processes.
I hope this focused approach helps readers build a familiarity with the background and physics required for understanding laser‑driven plasma physics. If you want to go further, there is a list of additional resources and books in Chapter 9. Plasma physics is a field that covers a wide range of phenomena, processes and theoretical and computational challenges that still remain relevant and exciting today. What begins as a simple kinetic theory of charged particles can lead to a rich and complex description of this remarkable state of matter.

title: 2  Magneto-Hydrodynamics
text:
2.1 The Kinetic Theory of Plasmas
This chapter will introduce the important theoretical background and equations lying at the foundation of plasma physics. The plasma state, often referred to as the fourth state of matter, is characterised as a macroscopically quasi-neutral ensemble of charged particles; this is an ionised gas of freely moving electrons and ions where local charge imbalances are rapidly neutralised due to high mobility of charges, maintaining overall electrical neutrality on large scales. As such the electromagnetic interactions between the charged particles lead to long-range electromagnetic forces as well as the short range collisional forces. These interactions give rise to collective behaviour, which is central to many phenomena observed in laboratory, space, and astrophysical plasmas.
Kinetic theory will be the framework used to describe the dynamics of this state of matter; this theory describes the evolution of distribution functions in phase space. The starting point of this chapter will be the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck (VFP) equation and an introduction to the kinetic theory of plasmas, following with the derivation of the single fluid model of magneto-hydrodynamics (MHD). The VFP equation bridges the microscopic particle dynamics with macroscopic fluid models, providing a rigorous basis for deriving fluid equations through appropriate moment hierarchies and closure approximations. The MHD framework is especially useful for modelling large-scale, low-frequency phenomena such as magnetic confinement, plasma instabilities, and wave propagation. However, it neglects kinetic effects such as Landau damping, velocity-space instabilities, and collisionless wave-particle interactions, which can be critical in weakly collisional or high-frequency regimes. For these cases, kinetic models or extended fluid models (such as two-fluid or Hall-MHD models) are more appropriate.
A plasma is a statistical ensemble of ions and electrons that undergo long-range interactions via the Lorentz force \[
\textbf{F}=q(\textbf{E}+\textbf{v}\times\textbf{B}),
\] for some particle of charge \(q\). Though the electrostatic force of a single particle has an infinite range, the collective nature of an ensemble of charged particles means any charge imbalance will experience shielding from oppositely-charged particles. Considering the thermal motion of charged particles in the electric potential of a charge imbalance, this effect defines a characteristic length scale over which shielding occurs known as the Debye length \[
\lambda_D=\left(\frac{\epsilon_0 k_b T_e}{n_e e^2}\right)^{1/2},
\] where the electron number density \(n_e\) is in \(m^{-3}\) and the electron temperature \(T_e\) is expressed in units of Kelvin. Physically the Debye length can be considered the length scale of the screening of bare charges in plasma. Beyond a sphere of radius \(\lambda_D\), the Debye sphere, the plasma can be considered quasi-neutral.
The electric fields of this ensemble self-consistently adapt to the charge environment of the collection of particles. As a result, imbalances in charge excite plasma oscillations with a characteristic frequency that act to re-establish quasi-neutrality. This frequency is known as the plasma frequency \[
\omega_p=\left(\frac{n_e e^2}{m_e \epsilon_0}\right)^{1/2}.
\] where \(n_e\) is the electron number density, \(e\) is the elementary charge, \(m\) is the electron mass, and \(\epsilon_0\) is the vacuum permittivity. The plasma frequency defines a timescale above which the plasma can be considered quasi-neutral. This frequency sets a fundamental timescale for charge separation dynamics in the plasma. For timescales longer than \(\omega_p^{-1}\), charge imbalances tend to be rapidly smoothed out due to the collective response of the electrons, restoring quasi-neutrality—a state in which the densities of positive and negative charges are nearly equal on macroscopic scales. Therefore, in many practical scenarios, especially in low-frequency or large-scale plasma behaviour, the plasma can be effectively treated as a quasi-neutral medium.
These two parameters define the length and timescales above which we can define the collective statistical state called a plasma. The most accurate model to describe this N-particle system would be the Liouville equation under the action of a self-consistent electromagnetic field. However, the requirements to solve a system in \(6N\) dimensional phase space is not necessary or possible. Instead this collective behaviour is best described in terms of the distribution function, \(f(\textbf{x},\textbf{v},t)\), which represents the particle density in the 6-dimensional single-particle phase space. The evolution of distribution functions is the subject of kinetic theory. A plasma is described kinetically by the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck (VFP) equation \[
\frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial t} + \textbf{v}_\alpha\cdot\nabla f_\alpha + \frac{q_\alpha}{m_\alpha}(\textbf{E}+\textbf{v}_\alpha\times \textbf{B})\cdot\nabla_v f_\alpha = \left( \frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial t} \right)_{coll}
\] for a species \(\alpha\). The collision operator on the right-hand-side is the Fokker-Planck operator which will be introduced in Chapter 3. There is a VFP equation for each species present in the plasma, and represents the conservation of probability in phase space. The collision term on the right-hand-side takes the form of the Fokker-Planck operator, which determines how the Coulomb collisions between particles in the plasma influence the evolution of the distribution function. Intuitively while one would think the electric fields of every particle should influence the evolution of the plasma, Debye shielding allows the separation of the electromagnetic field into a microscopic, fluctuating component that forms part of the collision term, and macroscopic fields that sit in the left hand side of the VFP equation.
The most accurate approach starts straight from the VFP model of a plasma and solves for the electron and ion distribution functions. However, one often resorts to reduced models that retain essential physics while offering computational or analytical tractability. One can start with a simpler hydrodynamic approximation where instead of tracking the full distribution function, one models the plasma using macroscopic moments such as density, velocity, and pressure. Very collisional plasmas can be assumed to have a distribution function close to a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, which for electrons is \[
f_m=n_e\left(\frac{1}{2\pi v_{th}^2}\right)^{3/2}\exp{\left(-\frac{v^2}{2 v_{th}^2}\right)},
\] with the standard deviation being the thermal speed defined as \(v_{th}=\sqrt{k_b T_e/m_e}\). Given this near-equilibrium form, one can derive a set of fluid equations by taking moments of the VFP equation. This allows the use of a fluid description which can be derived by considering a small deviation from equilibrium, this fluid model is known as magneto-hydrodynamics.

title: 2  Magneto-Hydrodynamics
text:
2.2 Moments of the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck Equation
Deriving MHD from kinetic theory consists of taking moments of the VFP equation. These moments are the macroscopic quantities found by taking averages over the distribution function; in particular the conserved quantities or mass, momentum and energy. However in taking successive moments, each moment equation couples to the next. To create a closed system of equations, transport relations must be found that couple to a lower-order moment; in MHD this is achieved with the Fokker-Planck collision term. For a macroscopic fluid model the equations must describe the relationships between macroscopic quantities. The moments are found by multiplying the distribution function by successive velocity variables \(v_i\) and integrating over the whole of velocity space. The first few moments below are number density, fluid velocity, total energy density, heat and enthalpy flux and the stress tensor, respectively \[
\begin{align}
n(\textbf{r},t) &=\int f(\textbf{r},\textbf{v},t)d^3 v, \\
\textbf{V}(\textbf{r},t)&=\langle\textbf{v}\rangle =\frac{1}{n} \int \textbf{v} f(\textbf{r},\textbf{v},t)d^3 v, \\
\mathcal{E}(\textbf{r},t)&= \frac{1}{2} m n \langle v^2\rangle= \frac{1}{2}m\int v^2 f(\textbf{r},\textbf{v},t)d^3 v, \\
\textbf{q}(\textbf{r},t)&= \frac{1}{2}m n \langle w^2 \textbf{v}\rangle = \frac{1}{2}m \int w^2 \textbf{v} f(\textbf{r},\textbf{v},t)d^3 v, \\
\sigma_{ij}&= m n\langle w_i w_j\rangle = m \int w_i w_j f(\textbf{r},\textbf{v},t)d^3 v,
\end{align}
\] where \(w\) is the ‘anomalous velocity’, the deviation from the mean velocity, \(\textbf{w}=\textbf{v}-\textbf{V}\). In general the \(n^{th}\) moment of the distribution function is \[
\langle \textbf{v}^n\rangle = \frac{1}{n}\int \textbf{v}^n f(\textbf{r},\textbf{v},t)d^3 v.
\] Taking the first moment of the VFP equation for species \(\alpha\) yields the continuity equation \[
\frac{\partial n}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot (n \textbf{V})=\int \left( \frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial t} \right)_{coll} d^3v.
\] If there are no collisions that lead to a change in particle number of the species in question i.e ionisation or recombination, then \[
\int \left( \frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial t} \right)_{coll} d^3v=0.
\] The second moment can be found by multiplying the VFP equation by \(m\textbf{v}\) and following the same routine to give \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(mn V_j) + \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}(mn \langle v_i v_j\rangle ) -q n(E_j+(\textbf{V}\times\textbf{B})_j)= \int mv_j \left( \frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial t} \right)_{coll} d^3v.
\] To put this equation into a more familiar form note that the velocity \(\textbf{V}\) is the sum of the average (\(\textbf{V}\)) and `anomalous’ (\(\textbf{w}\)) parts \(\textbf{v}=\textbf{w}+\textbf{V}\), therefore \[
\begin{align}
\langle v_i v_j\rangle &= \langle (V_i + w_i)(V_j+w_j)\rangle \\
&= V_iV_j + \langle w_i w_j\rangle,
\end{align}
\] remembering \(\langle w_i\rangle=0\) as it is an anomalous, random fluctuation. Putting this into the equation and invoking the continuity equation allows the equation to be written \[
mn\frac{\partial V_i}{\partial t} + mn V_j \frac{\partial V_i}{\partial x_j} - qn(E_i+(\textbf{V}\times\textbf{B})_i)=-\frac{\partial \sigma_{ij}}{\partial x_j}+\int mv_i \left( \frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial t} \right)_{coll} d^3v.
\] The stress tensor can be written in terms of the isotropic pressure \(p\) and anisotropic stress \(\pi_{ij}\), \[
\sigma_{ij}=p\delta_{ij}+\pi_{ij}.
\] If the plasma is inviscid the anisotropic part (\(\pi_{ij}\)) is ignored and what is left is the momentum equation, \[
mn\frac{\partial \textbf{V}}{\partial t} + mn \textbf{V}\cdot\nabla \textbf{V} - qn(\textbf{E}+\textbf{V}\times\textbf{B})=-\nabla p+\textbf{R}.
\] The collision term has been shortened to \[
\textbf{R}=\int m\textbf{v} \left( \frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial t} \right)_{coll}d^3v.
\] Which satisfies \[
\begin{align}
    \textbf{R}=\sum_\beta \textbf{R}_{\alpha \beta},
\end{align}
\] since there are collisions with all other species. Also note self-collisions conserve momentum, hence \(\textbf{R}_{\alpha \alpha}=0\).
The third equation to be derived is the energy equation. One can formulate the energy equation in terms to the total thermal energy, but here we will derive the energy equation in terms of temperature. This is an arbitrary choice, and one taken because heat flow is expressed in terms of temperature gradients. Since Boltzmann’s constant \(k_b\) is always associated with the temperature \(T\), a change of units for temperature allows one to absorb it into the definition of \(T\), so it now appears in units of energy rather than degrees Kelvin (thus \(k_b T \rightarrow T\) from here on). Using the following definitions of thermal energy density, kinetic energy density and thermal heat flow, \[
\begin{align}
&\mathcal{E_T} = \frac{1}{2}mn\langle w^2\rangle = \frac{3}{2}nT, \\
&\mathcal{E}_K = \frac{1}{2}n m V^2, \\
&\textbf{q}'= \frac{1}{2}m n \langle w^2 \textbf{w}\rangle = \frac{1}{2}m \int w^2 \textbf{w} f(\textbf{r},\textbf{v},t)d^3 v,
\end{align}
\] and the ideal gas law equation of state \[
p=nT.
\] The temperature equation can be written \[
\frac{3}{2}n\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} + \textbf{V}\cdot\nabla T\right) +\nabla \cdot \textbf{q}'+p\nabla \cdot\textbf{V} =Q,
\] where the collision terms have been shortened to Q by using \[
\begin{align}
Q=\frac{1}{2}m\int v^2 \left( \frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial t} \right)_{coll} d^3v- \textbf{R}\cdot \textbf{V}.
\end{align}
\] If this analysis is done for both the electron and ion VFP equations the result is a set of six transport equations, three each for the electrons and ions. \[
\begin{gather}
\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot (n_e \textbf{V}_e)=0, \\
m_e n_e\frac{\partial \textbf{V}_e}{\partial t} + m_en_e \textbf{V}_e\cdot\nabla \textbf{V}_e +en_e(\textbf{E}+\textbf{V}_e\times\textbf{B})=-\nabla p_e+\textbf{R}_e,\\
\frac{3}{2}n_e\frac{\partial T_e}{\partial t} + \frac{3}{2}n_e\textbf{V}_e\cdot\nabla T_e +\nabla \cdot \textbf{q}'_e+p_e\nabla \cdot\textbf{V}_e =Q_e,\\
\frac{\partial n_i}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot (n_i \textbf{V}_i)=0, \\
m_i n_i\frac{\partial \textbf{V}_i}{\partial t} + m_i n_i \textbf{V}_i\cdot\nabla \textbf{V}_i - Zen_i(\textbf{E}+\textbf{V}_i\times\textbf{B})=-\nabla p_i+\textbf{R}_i,\\
\frac{3}{2}n_i\frac{\partial T_i}{\partial t} + \frac{3}{2}n_i\textbf{V}_i\cdot\nabla T_i +\nabla \cdot \textbf{q}'_i+p_i\nabla \cdot\textbf{V}_i =Q_i.
\end{gather}
\]
These transport equations, derived from the moments of the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation, form the foundation of the two-fluid plasma model, where electrons and ions are treated as separate interacting fluids. This approach retains more kinetic information than single-fluid MHD and is capable of capturing important effects such as electron-ion temperature differences, charge separation on small scales, and species-specific transport phenomena. Notably, the momentum equations for each species include both electromagnetic forces and collisional momentum exchange, represented by \(R_e\) and \(R_i\), which ensure conservation of total momentum across the system. Similarly, the energy equations include heat flux terms \(q_e'\) and \(q_i'\), which account for non-local transport of thermal energy due to the random motion of particles—effects that are especially important in weakly collisional or magnetised plasmas. The collision source terms \(Q_e\) and \(Q_i\) represent both energy exchange between species and dissipative heating mechanisms. In the limit of high collisionality and scale separation, these equations reduce to the single-fluid MHD model through a series of asymptotic approximations, but retaining them in full is crucial for modelling high-frequency dynamics, small-scale structures, or plasmas with low collisionality such as those found in the solar wind or magnetic fusion devices.

title: 2  Magneto-Hydrodynamics
text:
2.3 The Single Fluid Model
Thus far the plasma can be treated as two inter-penetrating fluids. Using the fact that the mass of the electron is much lower than that of a proton, it is justifiable to ignore the electron inertia and define a simpler single fluid model with fluid velocity \(\textbf{V}\) and density \(\rho\). Since \(m_i>>m_e\), the total plasma density is dominated by the ion density, \[
\rho=m_i n_i+m_e n_e \approx m_i n_i.
\] Likewise the total momentum then becomes the ion momentum, with the fluid velocity the ion velocity (henceforth the subscript on \(\textbf{V}_i\) will be dropped) \[
\rho\textbf{V}=m_i n_i \textbf{V}_i+m_e n_e\textbf{V}_e \approx m_i n_i \textbf{V}_i.
\] Quasi-neutrality implies the number density of electrons and ions follows the relationship \[
Zn_i=n_e,
\] where Z is the average ionisation of the plasma. If the two continuity equations are summed, the above approximations yield the total continuity equation \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot (\rho\textbf{V})=0.
\] Considering charge continuity, one can define the charge density, current and relative velocity \[
\begin{align*}
\rho_c&=e(Zn_i-n_e),\\
\textbf{U}&=\textbf{V}_e-\textbf{V}_i,\\
\textbf{j}&=\rho_c \textbf{V}_i-en_e\textbf{U},
\end{align*}
\] which means the charge continuity equation is \[
\frac{\partial \rho_c}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot \textbf{j}=0.
\] Since the plasma is quasi-neutral, \(\rho_c << en_e\) and so \[
\textbf{j}=-en_e \textbf{U},
\] which gives the quasi-neutrality condition \[
\nabla\cdot\textbf{j}=0.
\] The single fluid momentum equation is found by taking the sum of the fluid momentum equations. This equation can be simplified by first applying quasi-neutrality which removes the electric field term. Momentum is conserved in collisions, so the collision terms cancel because they satisfy \[
\textbf{R}_e=-\textbf{R}_i.
\] After neglecting electron inertia and defining total pressure \(p=p_e+p_i\) and using the definition of the current, the momentum equation is \[
\rho\frac{\partial \textbf{V}}{\partial t} + \rho \textbf{V}\cdot\nabla \textbf{V} =-\nabla p+\textbf{j}\times\textbf{B}.
\]
An important aspect of this single-fluid approximation is that it still captures the essential electromagnetic coupling through the Lorentz force term \(\textbf{j} \times \textbf{B}\), despite having neglected electron inertia and simplified the multi-species dynamics. This term governs how magnetic fields influence plasma motion and is central to many MHD phenomena such as Alfvén waves, magnetic pressure, magnetic tension, and magnetic reconnection. The simplification of the current density \(\textbf{j}=−en_e\textbf{U}\) also implicitly retains information about the relative drift between electrons and ions, which is critical for resistive effects and Hall currents. While the electric field disappears from the momentum equation under quasi-neutrality, it re-emerges through Ohm’s law, which is derived separately and determines the evolution of the electric field in terms of macroscopic fluid quantities. Therefore, even though the two-fluid model has been reduced to a single-fluid form, key physics related to charge transport, magnetic field evolution, and force balance remain embedded in the resulting MHD equations.

title: 2  Magneto-Hydrodynamics
text:
2.4 The Energy Equation
For this single fluid model the energy equation can be derived by summing the energy equations for the electrons and ions. The total thermal energy density is given by the sum of the electron and ion thermal energy densities. However the ion thermal energy density is negligible compared to the electron thermal energy density in these plasma regimes. The electron temperature dominates the thermal energy in and the heat flow is dominated by the electron heat flow. Thus ion temperature can be ignored. To find the appropriate energy equation one begins with the electron energy equation and restate the current definition to remove the electron velocity. Then one uses the heat flow in the ion frame \[
\textbf{q}=\textbf{q}'-\frac{5}{2en_e}p_e\textbf{j}.
\] The total energy equation for the plasma relies on the cold ion approximation. The cold ion approximation (where \(T_i\approx 0\)) can be used because in high-energy-density plasmas the thermal energy is dominated by the electron temperature, and the heat flow dominated by the electron heat flow. In this approximation the ion pressure can also be ignored \(p_i\approx 0\) and the ion energy equation is removed. In this case the total thermal energy of the plasma is held by the electrons. The energy equation is then \[
\frac{3}{2}n_e\left(\frac{\partial T_e}{\partial t}+\textbf{V}\cdot\nabla T_e\right)+p\nabla \cdot\textbf{V}+\nabla \cdot \textbf{q}=\textbf{R}_e\cdot\textbf{j}/e n_e.
\] This simplified energy equation reflects a common and practical assumption in modelling high-energy-density or laser-produced plasmas, where electrons are rapidly heated (e.g., via laser absorption or collisional processes) while ions remain comparatively cold due to their larger mass and slower thermal response. The cold ion approximation significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy in regimes where electron thermodynamics dominate energy transport and pressure forces. The heat flux vector, corrected for the frame shift to the ion rest frame, captures the non-ideal transport of thermal energy due to electron thermal conduction which is the dominant mechanism for energy redistribution in such plasmas. The right-hand side term \(\textbf{R}_e\cdot\textbf{j}/e n_e\) represents collisional heating of electrons by resistive dissipation, sometimes referred to as Ohmic heating, where electron-ion collisions convert electromagnetic energy into thermal energy. This coupling is crucial in understanding energy deposition in plasma. Despite its simplicity, this energy equation retains essential physics necessary for modelling thermal evolution and energy transport in many laboratory and astrophysical plasmas.

title: 2  Magneto-Hydrodynamics
text:
2.5 Maxwell’s Equations
The defining property of plasmas relative to other fluids is their response to electromagnetic fields. Plasmas act as both a medium carrying fields and as a source of fields through the motion of charged particles. The electromagnetic fields in a plasma are governed by Maxwell’s equations, which describe how electric and magnetic fields interact with charges and currents. In the context of plasmas, these equations must be modified to account for coupling the fields and the plasma dynamics. Maxwell’s equations in differential form are given by \[
\begin{align}
&\nabla \cdot \textbf{E}=\frac{\rho_c}{\epsilon_0}, \\
&\nabla \cdot \textbf{B}=0, \\
&\nabla \times \textbf{E}=-\frac{\partial \textbf{B}}{\partial t}, \\
&\nabla \times \textbf{B}=\mu_0 \textbf{j}+\mu_0\epsilon_0\frac{\partial \textbf{E}}{\partial t}.
\end{align}
\] As the plasma is quasi-neutral, the charge density on a scale above that of the Debye length will be zero, \(\rho_c =0\). In addition, the temporal regime of interest in single-fluid plasma models is that described by low-frequency phenomena, where the characteristic timescale is much longer than the plasma period, i.e \(\partial_t<<\omega_p\). This means the displacement field in the Ampere-Maxwell law can be ignored since the timescale of the plasma dynamics is far below the fast electron plasma period (\(1/\omega_p\)) timescale. Under these simplifying assumptions Maxwell’s equations in plasmas become \[
\begin{align}
&\nabla \cdot \textbf{B}=0, \\
&\nabla \times \textbf{E}=-\frac{\partial \textbf{B}}{\partial t}, \\
&\nabla \times \textbf{B}=\mu_0 \textbf{j}.
\end{align}
\] However, it is important to note that this approximation breaks down at small scales near the Debye length, or in phenomena involving double layers, sheaths, or fast electromagnetic waves, where full Maxwell-Vlasov or two-fluid treatments become necessary. In the MHD context, these reduced equations still capture essential magnetic dynamics such as flux freezing, inductive field generation, and magnetic pressure/tension forces, making them a cornerstone of plasma fluid modelling.

title: 3  Closure and Collisions
text:
3.1 Collisions in Plasmas
In the previous chapter we derived a set of fluid equations for a plasma; however, the system of equations is not closed because there is no equation coupling the heat flow \(\textbf{q}\) to a lower-order moment, or an expression for the collision term \(\textbf{R}_e\). The conventional approach to close the system of equations is to use the Chapman-Enskog expansion. In this approach the distribution function is assumed to be approximately Maxwellian with only a small deviation; this approximation holds very well in strongly collisional plasmas because collisions drive the distribution towards equilibrium. This closure problem arises because the moment hierarchy derived from the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation is infinite: each moment equation depends on the next higher-order moment, preventing a self-contained solution without additional assumptions. The Chapman-Enskog expansion provides a systematic method to truncate this hierarchy by expressing higher-order moments (such as heat flux and stress) as functions of lower-order quantities (like density, velocity, and temperature gradients). Physically, this corresponds to modelling the effects of irreversible transport processes in terms of macroscopic gradients and plasma parameters, such as viscous momentum transport, thermal conduction, and resistive dissipation. The resulting closure relations allow the introduction of classical transport coefficients, such as electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, and viscosity, which are fundamentally governed by collisional dynamics.
The collisions between charged particles in a plasma are Coulomb collisions, where a charged particle is scattered by the electrostatic field of another charged particle. Considering the single-particle motion of an electron in an electrostatic field, the collision frequency of an electron with speed \(v\) from ions in a plasma is \[
\nu_{ei}(v)=\frac{n_i\Gamma_{ei}}{v^3}=\frac{3 \sqrt{\pi}}{4 \tau_{ei}} \left(\frac{v_{th}}{v}\right)^3,
\] with the factor \(\Gamma_{ei}\), collision time \(\tau_{ei}\), Coulomb logarithm \(\ln \Lambda\) and thermal speed \(v_{th}\) defined as \[
\begin{align}
    \Gamma_{ei}&=\frac{Z^2 e^4 \ln{\Lambda}}{4\pi \epsilon_0^2 m_e^2},\\
    \tau_{ei}&=\frac{12\pi^{3/2}}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{\sqrt{m_e} T_e^{3/2} \epsilon_0^2}{n_i Z^2 e^4 \ln \Lambda},\\
    \ln{\Lambda}&=\ln(4\pi n_e \lambda^3_D),\\
    v_{th}&=\sqrt{\frac{T_e}{m_e}}.
\end{align}
\] These expressions can be derived by considering the elastic scattering of an electron in the presence of electrostatic field from a static ion. The full calculation of the collision frequency will be omitted here, but can be found in any good description of the Rutherford scattering model. The velocity dependence of the collision frequency is of the order \(v^{-3}\); this means slow, low energy particles are highly collisional whereas fast particles are effectively collisionless. At the thermal speed, the temperature dependence of the collision frequency is of the order \(T_e^{-3/2}\). One can also define the mean free path of e-i collisions \(\lambda_{ei}\) to be \[
    \lambda_{ei}=v_{th}\tau_{ei}.
\] The collision frequencies for different species can be ordered by considering the masses of the particles, leading to a scaling that allows us to simplify our analysis of the collision operator. Comparing the collision frequencies of ion-ion, electron-electron and ion-electron collisions one can find they approximately follow the scaling \[
    \nu_{ee}\sim\nu_{ei}/\sqrt{2}>>\nu_{ii}\sim\sqrt{\frac{m_e}{m_i}}\nu_{ei}>>\nu_{ie}\sim\frac{m_e}{m_i}\nu_{ei}.
\] Since i-i and i-e collisions have a frequency much lower than e-i collisions (by factors \(\sqrt{m_e/m_i}\) and \(m_e/m_i\) respectively) it is possible to safely ignore them in approximations of transport and collisional effects on the distribution function. This argument cannot however be applied to electron-electron collisions so the e-e operator must be included.
The fact that electron-ion collisions dominate over ion-ion or ion-electron collisions justifies modelling collisional transport primarily through the electron dynamics, while treating ions as nearly collisionless for the purpose of heat and momentum transport. However, because electron-electron collisions efficiently redistribute energy among electrons and maintain a Maxwellian core distribution, their inclusion is essential for establishing valid closure relations and defining well-behaved macroscopic quantities like temperature and conductivity. This underlines the importance of using an accurate collision operator which properly captures the small-angle, cumulative nature of Coulomb interactions while distinguishing between self-collisions (e-e) and cross-species (e-i) collisions.

title: 3  Closure and Collisions
text:
3.2 The Fokker-Planck Collision Operator
For the plasmas in the regimes covered in this book, Coulomb collisions are considered to be small-angle, glancing collisions. This approximation is equivalent to Brownian motion because they represent stochastic corrections that drive the total distribution towards a Gaussian distribution. The operator that very accurately models such collisions in this regime is the Fokker-Planck operator \[
\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)_{coll}=-\frac{\partial}{\partial \textbf{v}}\left(\frac{\langle\Delta \textbf{v}\rangle f}{\Delta t}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\textbf{v}\partial\textbf{v}}\left(\frac{\langle \Delta \textbf{v}\Delta \textbf{v}\rangle f}{\Delta t}\right).
\] This operator is split into two terms that represent drift and diffusion of the distribution function through velocity space. To transform the Fokker-Planck operator into explicitly Coulomb-collision form, the Rosenbluth potentials \(H_\beta\) and \(G_\beta\) are used for species \(\beta\). The expressions \(\frac{\langle \Delta \textbf{v}\Delta \textbf{v}\rangle}{\Delta t}\) and \(\frac{\langle \Delta \textbf{v}\rangle}{\Delta t}\) are written in terms of these potentials thus \[
\begin{align}
    &\frac{\langle \Delta v_i \rangle}{\Delta t}=\Gamma_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\partial H_\beta}{\partial v_i},\\
    &\frac{\langle \Delta v_i \Delta v_j \rangle}{\Delta t}=\Gamma_{\alpha\beta} \frac{\partial G_\beta}{\partial v_i \partial v_j},\\
    &G_\beta(\textbf{v})=\int |\textbf{v}-\textbf{v}_\beta|f_\beta(\textbf{v}_\beta)d\textbf{v}_\beta,\\
    &H_\beta(\textbf{v})= \frac{m+m_\beta}{m_\beta}\int \frac{f_\beta(\textbf{v}_\beta)}{ |\textbf{v}-\textbf{v}_\beta|} d\textbf{v}_\beta,
\end{align}
\] for collisions between species \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). By using these forms the Rosenbluth form of the Fokker-Planck equation becomes \[
\left( \frac{\partial f_\alpha}{\partial t} \right)_{coll}= \Gamma_{\alpha\beta}\left[ - \frac{\partial}{\partial v_i}\left(f_\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial v_j} H_\beta \right) + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial v_i}\frac{\partial}{\partial v_j}\left( f_\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial v_i}\frac{\partial}{\partial v_j}G_\beta \right) \right].
\]
Furthermore, the cold ion approximation means a Maxwellian ion distribution is replaced with a Dirac delta \(f_i=n_i\delta(\textbf{v}_i)\) as the temperature (and thus the variance of the Maxwellian) of the ion distribution vanishes. The Rosenbluth potentials reduce to \[
\begin{align}
    &G_i(\textbf{v})=n_i v,\\
    &H_i(\textbf{v})=n_i/v.
\end{align}
\] The Fokker-Planck operator for electron-ion collisions reduces to the Lorentz scattering operator. \[
    \left( \frac{\partial f_e}{\partial t} \right)_{coll}= \frac{n_i\Gamma_{ei}}{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial v_i}\left[\left( \frac{v^2\delta_{ij}-v_i v_j}{v^3}\right) \frac{\partial f_e}{\partial v_j} \right].
\] This final form of the collision operator, known as the Lorentz operator, describes pitch-angle scattering representing the random deflection of electron velocities due to encounters with much heavier, stationary ions. It captures the dominant effect of electron-ion collisions in the cold-ion limit, where momentum transfer is primarily angular. Importantly, the Lorentz operator conserves particle number and respects the isotropy of the background ion distribution while driving the electron distribution function toward isotropy in velocity space.

title: 3  Closure and Collisions
text:
3.3 Closure
We now have everything required to close the system of equations. The Chapman-Enskog method proceeds with an approximately Maxwellian electron distribution function, \[
    f_e(\textbf{x},\textbf{v},t)=f_m+\delta f.
\] Spherical harmonics are used to take advantage of the form of the Lorentz scattering operator. This operator is linear and from Sturm-Liouville theory one can show it has spherical harmonic eigenfunctions. Expanding the distribution function in terms of spherical harmonics will simplify the collision term by replacing the velocity derivatives with angular derivatives. The spherical harmonics are defined as \[
    f_e(\textbf{x},\textbf{v},t)=\sum^\infty_{l=0}\sum^l_{m=-l}f_l^m(\textbf{x},v,t)P^m_l(\cos \theta)e^{im\phi},
\] The diffusive approximation truncates the spherical harmonic expansion after the \(l=1\) term such that the terms \(l>1\) are ignored. If \(f_0\) is further assumed to be a Maxwellian \(f_m\), this becomes the local approximation. Using this local approximation in the VFP equation, the expressions for the collisional force terms \(\textbf{R}\) and the heat flow \(\textbf{q}\) can be obtained from the moment definitions.
The momentum exchange terms \(\textbf{R}_e\) can be split into thermal and friction components \[
\textbf{R}=\textbf{R}_T + \textbf{R}_u.
\] these components are taken to be proportional to the temperature gradient and current respectively \[
\begin{align}
\textbf{R}_T &= - n_e \underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\cdot \nabla T, \\
\textbf{R}_u &= \underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\cdot \textbf{j} \frac{1}{e n_e}.
\end{align}
\] The transport coefficients \(\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\) and \(\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\) are the thermoelectric tensor and the resistivity tensor respectively. These coefficients are tensors because transport parallel and perpendicular to a magnetic field is not equal, leading to anisotropic transport.
The electron heat flux is defined in the moment definitions in Chapter 2, but the closure must consider the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic heat flow. Like the collision term \(\textbf{R}_e\) it is made up of two parts corresponding to thermal and frictional components \[
    \textbf{q}_e=\textbf{q}_u+\textbf{q}_T,
\] where \[
\begin{align}
    &\textbf{q}_u= - \underline{\underline{\mathbf{\beta}}}\cdot\textbf{j} \frac{T_e}{e},\\
    &\textbf{q}_T=-\underline{\underline{\mathbf{\kappa}}}\cdot\nabla T_e.
\end{align}
\]
The closure relations for \(\textbf{R}_e\) and \(\textbf{q}_e\) not only reflect the anisotropic nature of transport in a magnetised plasma, but are chosen based on symmetry properties rooted in thermodynamic theory. In particular, the structure of these relations is governed by the Onsager reciprocal relations, which state that the matrix of linear transport coefficients relating thermodynamic fluxes (like current and heat flow) to their conjugate forces (like electric field and temperature gradient) must be symmetric under time-reversal invariance, provided the microscopic dynamics obey that symmetry. This implies that the cross-coupling terms between current and temperature gradient must satisfy \(\underline{\underline{\mathbf{\beta}}}=\underline{\underline{\mathbf{\beta}}}^T\), and similarly for the other transport tensors. Physically, this symmetry means that the same mechanism responsible for generating a current by a thermal gradient (the thermoelectric effect) also produces a heat flux in response to an electric current (the Peltier effect), with equal efficiency in linear response. In a magnetised plasma, the tensors take on a more complicated tensorial form, but Onsager symmetry still applies if the magnetic field. These properties not only constrain the allowed forms of the transport tensors but also ensure thermodynamic consistency and energy conservation in the resulting fluid model.
These expressions close the system of equations, however the exact forms of the magnetised transport coefficients \(\underline{\underline{\mathbf{\alpha}}},\underline{\underline{\mathbf{\beta}}},\underline{\underline{\mathbf{\kappa}}}\) must now be specified. The introduction of the transport tensors marks the final step in closing the fluid system, but their full specification depends critically on the magnetic field strength and orientation.

title: 3  Closure and Collisions
text:
3.4 Ohm’s Law
The final component for a fully-closed system of equations is an equation linking the electric field to the rest of the plasma parameters. This is known as Ohm’s law, which plays the role of the electron momentum equation, but is derived by ignoring electron inertia and incorporating the form of the collision term \(	extbf{R}_e\). The result is the generalised Ohm’s law \[
e n_e(	extbf{E}+	extbf{V}	imes	extbf{B})= -
abla p_e+ 	extbf{j}	imes	extbf{B} + rac{1}{en_e}\underline{\underline{ oldsymbol{\alpha}}}\cdot	extbf{j}-n_e\underline{\underline{ oldsymbol{ eta}}}\cdot 
abla T_e.
\] Each term on the right-hand side corresponds to a distinct physical effect that contributes to the electric field experienced in the fluid (ion) frame. The pressure gradient term \(-
abla p_e\) represents the electron pressure drive, often important in regions of strong compression or expansion, such as in shocks or reconnection layers. The Hall term \(	extbf{j}	imes	extbf{B}\) captures two-fluid effects arising from the relative motion between electrons and ions, and becomes significant in regimes where the current varies on length scales comparable to or smaller than the ion skin depth. The resistive term involving \(\underline{\underline{ oldsymbol{\alpha}}}\cdot	extbf{j}\) accounts for Ohmic dissipation, which converts kinetic energy into heat via electron-ion collisions, and dominates in dense, cold, or weakly magnetised plasmas. Lastly, the thermoelectric term \(\underline{\underline{ oldsymbol{ eta}}}\cdot 
abla T_e\) describes the Nernst effect and other related phenomena where temperature gradients drive electric fields or currents. In strongly magnetised plasmas, anisotropy in these tensor coefficients can lead to complex behaviours such as cross-field currents and magnetic field advection by electron heat flux. Ohm’s law thus serves not only to determine \(	extbf{E}\) for Faraday’s law, but also introduces the necessary coupling between the electric field, current density, and plasma parameters that is essential for a self-consistent description of magnetised plasma dynamics.

title: 3  Closure and Collisions
text:
3.5 The Single-Fluid Model
Finally, bringing together the results of the previous sections together, the set of equations that describe a single-fluid magnetised plasma is thus:
The Continuity Equation \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot (\rho\textbf{V})=0
\] The Momentum Equation \[
\rho\frac{\partial \textbf{V}}{\partial t} +\rho\textbf{V}\cdot\nabla\textbf{V} =-\nabla p_e +\textbf{j}\times\textbf{B}
\] Ohm’s Law \[
e n_e(\textbf{E}+\textbf{V}\times\textbf{B})= -\nabla p_e+ \textbf{j}\times\textbf{B} +\frac{1}{en_e}\underline{\underline{\mathbf{\alpha}}}\cdot\textbf{j}-n_e\underline{\underline{\mathbf{\beta}}}\cdot \nabla T_e
\] The Heat Flow Equation \[
\mathbf{q}_e=-\underline{\underline{\mathbf{\kappa}}}\cdot\nabla T_e - \underline{\underline{\mathbf{\beta}}}\cdot\textbf{j} \frac{T_e}{e}
\] The Energy Equation \[
\frac{3}{2}n_e\left(\frac{\partial T_e}{\partial t}+\textbf{V}\cdot\nabla T_e\right)+p_e\nabla \cdot\textbf{V}+\nabla \cdot \textbf{q}=\textbf{E}\cdot\textbf{j}
\] Maxwell’s Equations \[
\nabla \times \textbf{E}=-\frac{\partial \textbf{B}}{\partial t}
\] \[
\nabla \times \textbf{B}=\mu_0 \textbf{j}
\]

title: 4  Magnetised Transport
text:
4.1 The Transport Coefficients
Now that the system is closed, the next step is to understand the form of the transport coefficients in a magnetised plasma. This section will discuss the form of these coefficients, their derivation and the different phenomena that arise from them. Understanding these coefficients is critical for accurate modelling of plasma behaviour in contexts ranging from magnetic confinement fusion and space plasmas to inertial confinement experiments and astrophysical jets.
Acting under the Lorentz force, electrons in a magnetised plasma travel on circular orbits in the plain perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field \(\hat{\textbf{b}}\). These orbits have a radius \(r_L(=v/\omega_c)\), the Larmor radius and orbit at the Larmor or cyclotron frequency, \(\omega_c\), \[
\omega_c=\frac{e B}{m_e}.
\]
Electrons in a plasma are constantly performing Coulomb collisions with ions and other electrons. In classical plasma theory, transport is a collisional process and it is possible to parameterise the influence of the magnetic field in terms of a dimensionless parameter known as the Hall parameter \[
\chi =\omega_c\tau_{ei},
\] which is a product of the electron-ion collision time and the electron cyclotron frequency. This parameter is a measure of how magnetised the plasma is; when electrons undergo Coulomb collisions, they hop onto a different Larmor orbit. If the Hall parameter is low, (see Figure 4.1) the magnetic field does not deflect the electron far from its path between collisions, if the Hall parameter is large the electron is effectively ‘confined’ to a small region, with the electron performing potentially many full orbits between collisions.
The deviation from isotropic, unmagnetised transport is encapsulated in the dimensionless tensors \(\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^c,\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^c,\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^c\), \[\begin{align*}
&\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}=\frac{m_e n_e}{\tau_{ei}}\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^c,\\
&\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^c,\\
&\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}=\frac{n_e T_e \tau_{ei}}{m_e}\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^c.
\end{align*}\] When the plasma is completely unmagnetised, such that \(\chi\rightarrow 0\), the coefficients \(\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^c,\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^c\) become diagonal and \(\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^c\) vanishes. These correspond to the classical Spitzer-Härm transport coefficients. The Spitzer-Härm coefficients are isotropic and can be written in terms of the electron-ion mean free path \(\lambda_{ei}\), the electron-ion collision time \(\tau_{ei}\) and the electron temperature \(T_e\).
To better understand the effect the anisotropic, off-diagonal terms have on transport, these coefficients can be written in a geometry where the basis is set by the direction of the magnetic field. When a magnetic field is applied to a plasma, it defines a preferred direction, breaking the isotropy of transport processes in a plasma and turning the transport coefficients into tensors. The magnetic field direction is defined \[
\hat{\textbf{b}}=\frac{\textbf{B}}{|\textbf{B}|}.
\] Given this geometry it is possible to write the contraction of a general transport coefficient \(\underline{\underline{\eta}}\) with a driving gradient \(\textbf{s}\) as \[
\underline{\underline{\eta}}\cdot\textbf{s}=\eta_\parallel \hat{\textbf{b}}( \hat{\textbf{b}}\cdot\textbf{s})+\eta_\perp \hat{\textbf{b}}\times (\textbf{s}\times\hat{\textbf{b}})+\eta_\wedge \hat{\textbf{b}}\times\textbf{s}.
\] This splits the transport into three terms, parallel \(\eta_\parallel\), perpendicular \(\eta_\perp\) and cross-perpendicular \(\eta_\wedge\) to the magnetic field. These directions are illustrated in Figure 4.2.
A Cartesian tensor form for this contraction will be useful when transitioning to a numerical model,
\[
    \eta_{ij}=\eta_\parallel b_ib_j+\eta_\perp\left(\delta_{ij}-b_ib_j\right)+\eta_\wedge\epsilon_{ikj}b_k,
\] which in full matrix form is \[
\underline{\underline{\eta}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\eta_\perp+(\eta_\parallel-\eta_\perp)b^2_x && -\eta_\wedge b_z+(\eta_\parallel-\eta_\perp)b_x b_y && \eta_\wedge b_y +(\eta_\parallel-\eta_\perp)b_x b_z \\
\eta_\wedge b_z +(\eta_\parallel-\eta_\perp)b_x b_y && \eta_\perp+(\eta_\parallel-\eta_\perp)b^2_y && -\eta_\wedge b_x +(\eta_\parallel-\eta_\perp)b_y b_z \\
-\eta_\wedge b_y+(\eta_\parallel-\eta_\perp)b_x b_z && \eta_\wedge b_x +(\eta_\parallel-\eta_\perp) b_y b_z  && \eta_\perp +(\eta_\parallel-\eta_\perp) b^2_z
\end{pmatrix}
\]
The closure equations of the previous section were derived without the electron-electron collision operator. While the assumption of no electron collisions applies for high-Z plasmas, the effect must be considered for low-Z plasmas. Calculating the magnetised transport coefficients with a full electron-electron Fokker-Planck collision operator is not analytically feasible so correction factors based on numerical solutions or approximations have been developed to give expressions of the transport coefficients in terms of the dimensionless Hall parameter. These incorporate the influence of electron-electron collisions into the electron-ion collision coefficients. Further, these functional forms have explicit dependence on the Hall parameter, making them sensitive to the level of magnetisation. Figure 4.3 shows one scheme of coefficients as functions of the Hall parameter for \(Z=1\).
An important feature of these magnetised transport coefficients is their nonlinear dependence on the Hall parameter \(\chi\), which reflects the transition from isotropic to highly anisotropic transport as the plasma becomes increasingly magnetised. At low \(\chi\), all three coefficients \(\eta_\parallel, \eta_\perp, \eta_\wedge\)​ converge to their unmagnetised values, with \(\eta_\wedge\rightarrow 0\) and \(\eta_\perp\rightarrow\eta_\parallel\)​, consistent with isotropic (Spitzer-Härm) transport. However, as \(\chi\) increases, strong differences emerge: \(\eta_\parallel\)​ remains largely unchanged since transport along the magnetic field is unaffected by gyration while \(\eta_\perp\)​ drops significantly, often scaling as \(∼1/\chi^2\) in the strongly magnetised limit. Meanwhile, the cross-field (Hall-like) coefficient \(\eta_\wedge\)​ grows and typically peaks near \(\chi∼1\), where magnetic and collisional timescales are comparable, before decreasing more slowly. This leads to phenomena such as Nernst advection and Righi-Leduc heat flow, where thermal energy or magnetic flux is transported across field lines due to temperature gradients. These effects are particularly pronounced in high-energy-density plasmas, such as those encountered in inertial confinement fusion or laser–plasma interactions, where steep gradients and strong magnetic fields coexist. Understanding and quantifying this anisotropy is essential not only for accurate theoretical modelling but also for designing experiments and interpreting measurements in magnetised plasma environments.

title: 4  Magnetised Transport
text:
4.2 Magnetised Transport Phenomena
The magnetised form of the transport coefficients greatly complicates the possible behaviour with more terms and the appearance of thermoelectric transport \(\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\) in Ohm’s law. This section will discuss the different phenomena that appear out of these tensor coefficients.

4.2.1 Diffusive and Righi-Leduc Heat Flow
With a parallel, perpendicular and cross-perpendicular decomposition, the heat flow splits into three parts \[
    \textbf{q}_T=-\kappa_\parallel \nabla_\parallel T_e - \kappa_\perp\nabla_\perp T_e - \kappa_\wedge\textbf{b}\times\nabla T_e.
\] The first two terms are diffusive heat flow and the third term is the Righi-Leduc heat flow. The diffusive nature is made clear by incorporating heat flow into the energy equation. If we look only at the time derivative and heat flow divergence terms, the result is a diffusion equation \[
\frac{3}{2}n_e\frac{\partial T_e}{\partial t}=\nabla\cdot\left(\kappa_\parallel \nabla_\parallel T_e + \kappa_\perp\nabla_\perp T_e + \kappa_\wedge\textbf{b}\times\nabla T_e\right).
\]
The asymptotic forms for the perpendicular heat flow \(\kappa_\perp\) as \(\chi \rightarrow 0\) and \(\chi \rightarrow \infty\), \[
\begin{align}
    \kappa_\perp &= \frac{n_e \lambda_{ei}^2}{\tau_{ei}} \frac{128}{3\pi},& \chi << 1\\
    \kappa_\perp &= \frac{n_e \lambda_{ei}^2}{\tau_{ei}} \frac{13}{4 \chi^2},& \chi >> 1\\
    &=n_e \frac{r_L^2}{\tau_{ei}}\frac{13}{4}.
\end{align}
\] Using the length scale definition of the Hall parameter \(\chi=\lambda_{ei}/r_L\), at very high magnetisation the characteristic diffusive step-length switches from the electron-ion mean free path \(\lambda_{ei}\) to the Larmor radius \(r_L\). The Righi-Leduc heat flow \(\textbf{q}_\wedge\) acts perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the temperature gradient. It deflects the flow of thermal energy, rotating the temperature profile of the plasma in the plane perpendicular to the magnetic field. The Righi-Leduc heat flow can therefore dominate over the diffusive heat flow \(\textbf{q}_\perp\) when \(\chi\) is very large. In the regime of \(\chi>>1\), the perpendicular thermal conductivity \(\kappa_\perp \propto \kappa_\parallel /\chi^2\) and the Righi-Leduc conductivity \(\kappa_\wedge \propto \kappa_\parallel /\chi\).


4.2.2 Ettingshausen Heat Flow
The Ettingshausen heat flow is a thermoelectric heat flow that results from the \(\beta_\wedge\) term of the magnetised heat flow equation, \[
\textbf{q}_E=-\beta_\wedge \frac{T_e}{e} \textbf{b}\times\textbf{j}.
\] This flow is associated with the advection of temperature down magnetic field gradients. This is made clear when this term is substituted into energy equation and using Ampere’s law to get \[
\frac{3}{2}n_e\frac{\partial T_e}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot\left(\textbf{v}_E T_e\right)=0.
\] This is an advection equation for temperature with an advection velocity \[
\textbf{v}_E = -\frac{\beta_\wedge}{e \mu_0}\nabla B.
\] This term has been found to play a relatively minor role in experimental platforms, with other processes dominating the thermal transport. However, it is still important to consider in simulations of magnetised plasmas, particularly in regimes where the magnetic field is strong and the temperature gradients are steep.


4.2.3 The Nernst Effect
The Nernst effect likewise arises from the \(\beta_\wedge\) term. However, instead it represents an advection of magnetic fields down temperature gradients. This has been used to infer a relationship with diffusive heat flow, which has been used alongside non-local thermal transport models for non-local corrections to Nernst advection. When the thermoelectric term of Ohm’s law is substituted into Faraday’s law, one finds an advection equation \[
\frac{\partial \textbf{B}}{\partial t}=\nabla\times(\textbf{v}_N\times\textbf{B}),
\] with the characteristic velocity \[
    \textbf{v}_N=-\frac{\beta_\wedge \nabla T_e}{e B}.
\] Therefore the Nernst effect advects magnetic fields with velocity \(\textbf{v}_N\) down temperature gradients, concentrating the magnetic field in low temperature regions. The Nernst effect can play a significant role in compressing self-generated magnetic fields in high-energy-density experiements, suggesting this once-neglected effect should play a greater role in plasma physics.


4.2.4 Resistive Diffusion
In resistive MHD the term \(\frac{1}{en_e}\underline{\underline{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\cdot\textbf{j}\), in conjunction with Faraday’s and Ampere’s laws can be combined to give an advection-diffusion equation \[
\frac{\partial \textbf{B}}{\partial t}=\textbf{v}_\alpha\times(\nabla\times\textbf{B})+\frac{\alpha_\perp}{e^2 n_e^2 \mu_0}\nabla^2 \textbf{B},
\] with the advection velocity \[
\textbf{v}_\alpha=-\frac{1}{e^2 \mu_0}\nabla\left(\frac{\alpha_\perp}{n_e^2}\right).
\]
The second term on the right hand side refers to the resistive diffusion of the magnetic field. The advective term with velocity \(\textbf{v}_\alpha\) corresponds to the resistive advection of the magnetic field in regions where the resistivity is non-uniform. While small in general, the resistive advection can grow to be as fast as the frozen in flow near shock fronts.
These magnetised transport phenomena collectively illustrate how a magnetic field not only modifies the magnitude of classical transport but also fundamentally alters its geometry and symmetry. The presence of strong magnetic fields introduces cross-field effects (like Righi-Leduc and Nernst flows) that are absent in unmagnetised plasmas, and these effects can become dominant when the Hall parameter is large. Notably, the Nernst effect provides a powerful mechanism for redistributing magnetic energy, especially in laser-driven plasmas, where steep temperature gradients naturally occur. Likewise, the interplay between anisotropic conduction and resistive diffusion creates complex magnetic dynamics not captured by ideal MHD, including magnetic field steepening and flux accretion. These transport effects are not just theoretical curiosities as they have measurable consequences on plasma structure, energy confinement, and instabilities.

title: 4  Magnetised Transport
text:
4.3 Biermann Battery Magnetic Field Generation
Though not a result of the collisional transport terms, the Biermann battery effect is an important magnetic field generation mechanism arising from the electron pressure term in Ohm’s law. Though first discovered in the context of interstellar magnetic fields, the Biermann battery effect is significant in the regimes of laser-plasma interactions and has been used as a means to induce \(\sim 100 T\) magnetic fields with nanosecond laser pulses.
Considering the electric field determined by the electron pressure gradient (also known as the ambipolar electric field) in Ohm’s law \[
    \textbf{E}=-\frac{\nabla p_e}{en_e},
\] and using the ideal gas law \(p_e=n_e T_e\) with Faraday’s law, the Biermann magnetic field generation mechanism follows \[
    \frac{\partial \textbf{B}}{\partial t}=\frac{1}{e n_e} \nabla T_e\times\nabla n_e.
\]
From this expression, if the electron density and electron temperature fields have non-parallel gradients, a magnetic field will be induced via the Biermann battery effect. In laser-generated plasmas, energy deposition via a laser heating mechanism will locally heat a region of the plasma. With a very non-uniform density profile-as is common in laser-plasma interactions-magnetic field generation via this mechanism is one of the most significant sources of magnetic fields in experiments. Even if a magnetic field has not been imposed externally, this mechanism can magnetise the plasma, leading to magnetised transport terms.

title: 5  Non-Local Transport
text:
The conventional derivation of fluid theory relies on the truncation of the spherical harmonic expansion of the electron distribution function in velocity space, and the assumption that the isotropic part \(f_0\) is Maxwellian. This local approximation holds in the regime \(L_T>>\lambda_{ei}\), where the electron-ion collision mean-free-path \(\lambda_{ei} (\propto T_e^2)\) is much smaller than the temperature scale length \(L_T\), defined as
\[
    \frac{1}{L_T}=\frac{1}{T}\frac{d T}{d x}.
\] From this one can define the Knudsen number, \[
    Kn=\frac{\lambda_{ei}}{L_T}.
\]
This number quantifies the degree of ‘non-locality’, in the regime of \(Kn<<1\) the electrons in the plasma experience sufficient Coulomb collisions such that the distribution function is approximately Maxwellian and in local thermal equilibrium. This condition however is frequently violated in high-intensity laser-plasma interactions where the interaction can drive steep temperature gradients. Electrons with collisional mean-free paths greater than the scale length of the gradient (where \(L_T<<\lambda_{ei}\)), stream down the temperature gradient without thermalising to the local distribution. As a result there is an increase in these hotter electrons (coming from the tail of the distribution in a high temperature region) and a depletion in another region, resulting in non-Maxwellian distribution functions and the break-down of classical transport. This depletion of hot electrons in the tail of the distribution from the region of the temperature gradient leads to a lower peak heat flux than expected from the Spitzer-Harm approximation \(\textbf{q}_{sh}\), \[
     \textbf{q}_{sh} \propto - n_e \lambda_{ei} v_{th}\nabla T_e.
\] The familiar Fourier law-type heat flow should also break down at sharp temperature gradients such as shock fronts as the heat flow would diverge. The heat flow should saturate at approximately the free streaming heat flow \(\textbf{q}_F\); the heat flow if all the electrons moved at the thermal speed in the direction of the temperature gradient \[
\textbf{q}_F=\frac{1}{2}m_e n_e v_{th}^3\frac{\nabla T_e}{|\nabla T_e|}.
\]
A simple method of accounting for this reduction is to use a flux limiter \(f_l\), where the classical heat flow is reduced to some fraction of the free streaming heat flow, \[
\frac{1}{q(x)}=\frac{1}{q_{sh}(x)}+\frac{1}{f_l q_{F}}.
\]
This however does not capture the effect of pre-heat, where heat flow is present even before the temperature gradient. Most of the heat flow is carried by fast electrons with speeds 3 to \(5 v_{th}\). Since the mean free path grows as \(\lambda_{ei}\propto v^4\), the less collisional, non-local electrons are carrying the heat flow beyond the temperature gradient. An alternative non-local thermal transport model that can capture this effect is through a convolutional kernel. In one dimension, \[
    q(x)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty W(x,x')q_{sh}(x')dx'.
\]
The difficulty in flux-limited or convolutional models is that the choice of limiter or kernel is arbitrary, with no real physical basis for commonly used models, and some choosing them to fit experimental data. While these models are simple, a VFP approach is necessary to get correct results.
The reduction in thermal conductivity can also be cast in Fourier space for a temperature perturbation mode with wavenumber \(k\). This effectively recasts the peak thermal flux reduction as a reduction of thermal conductivity for small length scale structures. One such model uses a non-local conductivity suppression factor relating the Spitzer-Harm thermal conductivity \(\kappa_{sh}\) to the non-local thermal conductivity \(\kappa_{nonlocal}\) of the form \[
\frac{\kappa_{nonlocal}}{\kappa_{sh}}=\frac{1}{1+a (\sqrt{Z} k\lambda_{ei})^b},
\] with the parameters \(a,b\) obtained by fitting this function to a numerical VFP simulation. The result is a reduction in thermal conductivity for higher modes (high \(k\lambda_{ei}\)) meaning short-wavelength scale structures saw reduced conductivity.
When magnetic fields are present in a plasma, the Larmor radius can become comparable to the mean free path. In this highly magnetised regime the Larmor radius becomes the characteristic step-length of diffusive transport. Given that the Larmor radius grows as \(r_L \propto v\) and \(\lambda_{ei} \propto v^4\), the hotter electrons in the tail (with higher \(v\)) of the electron distribution can be relatively unmagnetised while the bulk electrons are magnetised. Under a sufficiently strong magnetic field the transport is localised in the plane perpendicular to the field, no matter how large \(\lambda_{mfp}\). This quenching of non-locality is borne out in a magnetised gas-jet experiments and kinetic simulations.
An important conceptual insight from non-local transport theory is that heat flow in plasmas is inherently non-diffusive when the characteristic electron path lengths approach or exceed macroscopic gradient scale lengths. In this regime, kinetic effects dominate, and classical transport theories like Spitzer-Härm become invalid. This leads to phenomena such as preheat, where heat energy arrives in colder regions before the arrival of the thermal front predicted by local models. Additionally, the shape of the electron distribution function becomes skewed, with an enhanced suprathermal tail and lower mid-range velocities which are a feature that strongly affects heat flux and electric field generation. These kinetic effects have downstream effects on hydrodynamic evolution, changing shock profiles, instability growth, and magnetic field dynamics. As such, accurate modeling of non-local transport is not merely a refinement but a necessity in systems with steep gradients, such as laser-produced plasmas, hohlraums, or astrophysical shocks. While reduced models like flux-limiters or convolution-based corrections are often used in hydrodynamic simulations due to their simplicity, they lack the self-consistency and predictive power of full kinetic treatments. Ultimately, the inclusion of non-local transport remains one of the key motivations for incorporating Vlasov-Fokker-Planck solvers or hybrid kinetic-fluid approaches in high-fidelity plasma simulation tools.

title: 6  Laser Theory
text:
6.1 The Helmholtz Equation
High-intensity lasers are a key tool in the field of plasma physics. They are used to create and probe plasmas, as well as to drive high-energy particle acceleration. The interaction of laser light with plasma is complex and requires a detailed understanding of both the laser propagation and the plasma response. This chapter will introduce the theory of long-pulse laser propagation and coupling to plasma, which is essential for understanding high-energy-density physics. We start with the primary assumptions and analysis of laser propagation, before deriving the unidirectional-or paraxial-laser model. The plasma coupling mechanisms of inverse bremmsstrahlung and the ponderomotive force will then be introduced before concluding with a brief description of some of the important laser-plasma interactions that occur in the regimes of interest to this plasma regime.
Laser light is a monochromatic coherent electromagnetic wave. The starting point is Maxwell’s electromagnetic wave equation. \[
c^2 \nabla^2 \textbf{E}-c^2 \nabla (\nabla \cdot \textbf{E})=\frac{1}{\epsilon_0}\frac{\partial\textbf{j}}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial^2 \textbf{E}}{\partial t^2}.
\]
Solving this equation exactly would be numerically too demanding because the spatial and temporal resolution requirements would be too great and are unnecessary for the nanosecond pulse duration, high-power lasers used in laser-plasma physics experiments. Several simplifying assumptions can be made to reduce this equation into the paraxial laser equation. The current in a plasma is determined by the flux of the electrons. The dielectric behaviour of the plasma can thus be found from the electron equation of motion. The simplified equation of motion required for the fast electron response to the laser field is \[
m_e\frac{\partial (n_e \textbf{V}_e)}{\partial t}=-e n_e\textbf{E} - m_e\nu_{ei}n_e \textbf{V}_e.
\] The high-frequency response of a plasma to the oscillating laser fields justifies dropping the pressure gradient term. The magnetic field term is ignored because unless the plasma is relativistic, it will be much smaller than the electric field contribution due to the factor \(\sim v/c\). Using the definition of the current in terms of electron velocity this can be recast as \[
\frac{\partial \textbf{j}}{\partial t}= \frac{e^2 n_e}{m_e}\textbf{E}-\nu_{ei}\textbf{j}.
\]
Unfortunately, in order to have a closed set of equations the collision term must be rewritten in terms of the electric field. In order to do this the current in the collision term is approximated as \[
\textbf{j}\approx-\frac{e n_e}{m_e \omega_l^2}\frac{\partial \textbf{E}}{\partial t},
\]
which only holds in the regime where the collision frequency \(\nu_{ei}\) is much less than the laser angular frequency \(\omega_l\). Therefore the wave equation can be written \[
c^2 \nabla^2 \textbf{E}=\frac{e^2 n_e}{\epsilon_0 m_e}\left(\textbf{E}+\frac{\nu_{ei}}{\omega_l^2}\frac{\partial \textbf{E}}{\partial t}\right)+\frac{\partial^2 \textbf{E}}{\partial t^2}.
\]
Given this describes a laser field, the electric field can be considered a product of the fast temporal oscillation at the laser angular frequency \(\omega_l\) and a slowly varying ‘envelope’ \(\textbf{E'}(\textbf{r})\), where in total \(\textbf{E}(\textbf{r})=\textbf{E'}(\textbf{r})e^{-i\omega_l t}\). It is not necessary to resolve the fast oscillation of the wave because the \(\omega_l\) timescale is much faster than the timescale of the plasma dynamics. It is possible to integrate out the fast motion, giving an equation for the envelope of the laser field. Time derivatives of \(\textbf{E'}\) are ignored as the envelope is assumed to be slowly varying.
It is here we make use of the paraxial approximation, whereby \(\textbf{k}\cdot\textbf{E}=0\). This limits the validity of this model to small angle refraction from the wavevector axis (to within \(\pm 15\) degrees). While large angle refraction does occur in plasmas, the setups within most experiments are securely within the small-angle regime. This approximation removes the \(\nabla \cdot \textbf{E}\) term in the wave equation. This leaves the Helmholtz equation \[
\nabla^2 \textbf{E'}+\frac{\omega_l^2}{c^2}\epsilon\textbf{E'}=0.
\] Where the dielectric function \(\epsilon\) is defined as \[
\epsilon=1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_l^2}+i\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_l^3}\nu_{ei},
\] when expressed in terms of the plasma frequency, \[
    \omega_p=\frac{e^2 n_e}{\epsilon_0 m_e}.
\]
This Helmholtz equation for the laser envelope provides a powerful and tractable model for simulating laser propagation in underdense and near-critical plasmas. The dielectric function \(\epsilon\) encodes both dispersive and absorptive effects of the plasma on the laser field. The real part of \(\epsilon\) governs wave refraction, with the index of refraction given by \(n=Re(\epsilon)\)​, while the imaginary part describes absorption, often referred to as inverse bremsstrahlung. This absorption mechanism dominates in dense, low-temperature plasmas where electron-ion collisions are frequent. The frequency dependence of \(\epsilon\) also reveals the cutoff condition: when \(\omega_p=\omega_l\)​, the dielectric function vanishes, and the wave is unable to propagate further. This defines the critical density surface, beyond which the laser cannot penetrate. This critical surface plays a key role in laser-plasma interactions, acting as the interface where laser energy is deposited and converted into plasma motion, heat, or magnetic field generation. Despite its simplifying assumptions, the Helmholtz model captures essential physics for laser beam propagation, refraction, and absorption in inhomogeneous plasmas and is widely used in both theoretical and numerical laser-plasma modeling.

title: 6  Laser Theory
text:
6.2 The Paraxial Laser Model
The paraxial laser model is a simplification of the Helmholtz equation and it is based on the assumption that the laser beam is nearly collimated, meaning that it does not diverge significantly as it propagates. This allows us to derive a simpler equation that captures the essential physics of laser propagation while ignoring higher-order effects. This is also a form of a slowly varying envelope approximation. It is possible to write the electric field of a linearly polarised wave \(\textbf{E'}\) in terms of the envelope \(\psi\) (the magnitude in the axis of polarisation) and the phase \(\phi(z)\). Without loss of generality the direction of propagation is chosen to be along the \(z\)-axis which gives \[
E'(r,z)=\psi(r,z)\exp i\phi(z).
\]
The field is linearly polarised so it can be expressed as a complex scalar field. The phase function \(\phi\) is chosen such that \[
\phi(z)=\frac{\omega_l}{c}\sqrt{\epsilon_a} z.
\] The factor \(\epsilon_a\) is the dielectric function at the axis (that is, \(r=0\)). This expression is plugged into the Helmholtz equation and the envelope is assumed to be slowly varying such that \[
|\partial_{zz}|<<|k\partial_z|.
\] This is equivalent to assuming the wavevector of the laser light is directed along z axis and any variation away from this direction is small. This yields the paraxial transport equation \[
2ik\sqrt{\epsilon_a}\partial_z \psi+\nabla^2_\perp \psi+k^2\left(\epsilon-\epsilon_a\right)\psi=0,
\] where the vacuum wavenumber \(k\) is \[
k^2=\frac{\omega_l^2}{c^2}.
\]
The paraxial transport equation allows one to use the intensity \(I\) of the laser field directly, calculated from the laser envelope \(\psi\) \[
    I=\frac{1}{2} c \epsilon_0 \eta |\psi|^2,
\] with the speed of light \(c\), the permitivity of a vaccum \(\epsilon_0\) and \(\eta\) is the refractive index, defined as \[
    \eta=\sqrt{1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_l^2}}.
\]

title: 6  Laser Theory
text:
6.3 Gaussian Optics
In a vacuum the paraxial equation has a cylindrically symmetric solution known as a Gaussian beam. This solution is a valuable approximation to many real-world beam profiles for the model of the laser pulse field before it enters a plasma. This solution is \[
\psi(r,z)=\psi_0 \frac{w_0}{w(z)}\exp\left(\frac{- r^2}{ w(z)^2}\right)\exp\left(-i k z  -\frac{i r^2}{2 R}+ i \phi (z)\right).
\] This solution is defined in terms of the following parameters, the beam waist size \[
w(z)=w_0\sqrt{1+\frac{z^2}{z_r^2}},
\] the beam radius of curvature \[
R(z)=z\left(1+\frac{z_r^2}{z^2}\right),
\] the Rayleigh length, \[
z_r=\frac{ k w_0^2}{2},
\] and the Gouy phase \[
\phi(z)=\arctan (\frac{z}{z_r}).
\]
A map of the real part of the laser envelope \(\psi\) can be found in Figure 6.1.
